title: Kernel-aware interleaved phase orchestrator for latency-sensitive requests
creator: Liam Chen
description:
Goal: reduce P95/P99 latency for short interactive requests (chat-style prefill + short decode) without regressing overall cluster throughput for long batched generation.

Background: Current allocator tends to coalesce work by phase (prefill vs decode) and by kernel affinity which improves throughput but can create long tails for small, latency-sensitive requests when they collide with large batched decodes. We need an orchestrator that can interleave micro-slices of latency-sensitive phases onto low-latency kernel paths while still preserving batch efficiency for throughput-heavy workloads.

Proposal: implement a Kernel-aware Interleaved Phase Orchestrator (KIPO) with three core components: 1) lightweight runtime kernel latency model that scores incoming slices by predicted kernel execution latency and attention sparsity; 2) micro-slice interleaver which fragments long phases into small opportunistic slices and schedules them on low-latency kernels where possible; 3) token-second fairness accounting to prevent starvation of large jobs (credit banking + soft reservations).

Key constraints: must integrate with existing kernel probing hooks, not require full model recompilation, and be safe to enable under a canary rollout. The orchestrator will expose two knobs: latencyBias (increases preference for low-latency kernels) and sliceGranularity (micro-slice size in tokens).

Success metrics: P95 latency for interactive requests down by >=15%, P99 down by >=10%, cluster throughput regression <=5% on mixed workloads. Cost neutral or improved unit token cost for latency tier customers.
updates: 2025-02-15 - Initial design spike: prototype scheduler state machine and simple kernel latency predictor using recent per-kernel tail metrics.

2025-02-20 - Microbenchmarks: on small-chat workload (avg 12 tokens prefill, 24 tokens decode) P95 improved 22% when routed to low-latency kernels; throughput drop ~2.7% on large-batch benchmark (512 tokens, batch size 8).

2025-02-24 - Design review with runtime team: agreed to use token-second accounting for fairness, avoid hard preemption of in-flight kernel work, add soft hedging to reduce tail impact on large requests.

2025-02-28 - Implementation: added kernel affinity hint to allocator and micro-slice splitter. New config flags: runtime.kipo.enabled and runtime.kipo.latencyBias. Started unit tests for slice reassembly and KV cache correctness across micro-slices.

2025-03-02 - Canary run on staging: routed 15% of interactive traffic. Observed P99 tail reduced 12% and P95 reduced 18% on canary instances. Noted a 3.1% total throughput regression on staging cluster when canary scaled to 40% — investigating batching fragmentation overhead.
2025-03-04 - Feedback from SRE: need metrics for credit-bank starvation and visibility into micro-slice preemption incidents. Added dashboard panels and trace tags for slice_id and kernel_hint.
Next steps: optimize micro-slice packing to reduce kernel invocation overhead, run larger mixed-workload perf experiments, prepare runtime-1.20 canary rollout plan with staged throttles.
acceptance_criteria: Automated unit and integration tests covering micro-slice split/reassembly and KV cache correctness pass
Canary shows P95 improvement >=15% for interactive workload on at least two instance types with throughput regression <=5%
Operational dashboards surface token-second accounting, per-kernel latency scores, and starvation alerts
Rollout plan documented with kill-switch and canary percent schedule
notes: Trade-offs: aggressive interleaving favors latency at the cost of some kernel-level batching; necessary to tune per-customer tier.
We observed that attention-sparse models benefit more from low-latency kernels; kernel predictor will use attention density signals when available.
Fallback: if micro-slice overhead exceeds benefit for certain models/hardware, fallback to phase-coalescing policy per route.
Owners: runtime scheduling (Ava), kernel selection (Ravi), perf experiments (Liam)
